Workup


## Approach Considerations

Leptospirosis diagnosis is primarily clinical and based on exposure history. Importantly, empiric antimicrobial therapy must be initiated immediately upon suspicion and should not be delayed for laboratory confirmation. \[5\]  Diagnostic strategy is time-dependent, utilizing nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) during the first week of symptoms (septicemic phase) and transitioning to serological methods thereafter (immune phase). \[1, 2\]

![eMedicine Logo](https://img.medscapestatic.com/pi/global/logos/emed/logo-emedicine77x17.svg)

[Next: Laboratory Studies](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/220563-workup#c8)

## Laboratory Studies

Routine laboratory evaluation provides vital indicators of disease severity and organ involvement. Common hematological findings include leukocytosis with a left shift and significant thrombocytopenia, which serves as a primary marker for severe disease and hemorrhagic risk. \[5, 6\]  Renal dysfunction is characterized by elevations in blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine, often accompanied by a unique early finding of hypokalemia and natriuresis due to impaired proximal tubular function. \[7\]  Hepatic involvement typically presents as jaundice with a disproportionate increase in serum bilirubin compared to modest elevations in transaminases, while markedly elevated creatine phosphokinase levels help distinguish leptospirosis from other tropical febrile illnesses like [malaria](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/221134-overview#). \[1, 5\]

Diagnostic confirmation requires pathogen-specific testing tailored to the duration of symptoms. During the initial septicemic phase (days 1 to 7), nucleic acid amplification tests or real-time PCR are preferred for detecting _Leptospira_ DNA in whole blood, serum, or cerebrospinal fluid. It has long been presumed that bacteremia precedes bacteriuria by up to 2 weeks and limits the utility of urine PCR early in illness. However a 2025 retrospective study examining data gathered over 6 years from 188 adults with leptospirosis in French Guiana suggests the opposite. Among those in whom urine PCR was performed early, the predicted probability of urine PCR positivity exceeded that of blood PCR as early as 4 days into onset of symptoms. Overall, in the first week of illness, sensitivity of urine PCR (84%) exceeded that of blood (70%), with no statistical impact by early antibiotic therapy. \[17, 18, 5, 6\]  Serological testing with the microscopic agglutination test remains the gold standard, though it is often retrospective, requiring a single titer of 800 or higher or a fourfold rise between acute and convalescent sera for confirmation. IgM enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) serves as a valuable screening tool starting late in the first week of illness, though positive results should be validated by the microscopic agglutination test (MAT) due to potential cross-reactivity. \[1, 5\]

In an effort to improve both access in the field and speed of diagnosis, point-of-care testing has demonstrated notable advances, such as recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) testing with 35 minute turnaround time and comparable sensitivity and specificity to PCR. \[17\]  A novel lateral flow immunoassay (Lepto-LF) outperforms IgM-ELISA and slide agglutination test from day 6 after onset of symptoms, while a microfluidic paper-based device achieves urinary detection limits as low as 1.5 fg/mL with a 15-minute turnaround. \[18, 19\]

CDC case definition provides specific laboratory criteria for classification. Confirmatory evidence includes the isolation of _Leptospira_ from a clinical specimen, a fourfold or greater increase in MAT titers between acute and convalescent specimens, a single titer of 800 or higher, or the detection of pathogenic _Leptospira_ DNA via PCR from a clinical specimen. Presumptive evidence is defined by a MAT titer of 200 or higher but less than 800, or the detection of IgM antibodies via ELISA or lateral flow assay in an acute phase specimen. \[6\]

## Imaging Studies

Imaging is a critical component of the diagnostic workup for leptospirosis, particularly for the early detection of life-threatening pulmonary involvement.

### Plain radiography

Chest radiography often reveals abnormalities even in the absence of overt respiratory symptoms. The most characteristic finding is a diffuse, bilateral, nonlobar distribution of small nodular densities, often described as a snowflake appearance. These lesions represent areas of alveolar hemorrhage and may rapidly progress to confluent consolidation or ground-glass opacities as the clinical state deteriorates. \[5, 8\]  While lower lobe involvement is common, the distribution is typically peripheral, helping to differentiate it from some other causes of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. \[10, 22\]

### CT

Chest CT is significantly more sensitive than standard radiography for identifying early interstitial lung injury and alveolar hemorrhage. Typical computed tomography findings include bilateral, multifocal ground-glass opacities and consolidations, often with a peripheral or peribronchial distribution. In patients with severe leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome, computed tomography may demonstrate dense consolidations consistent with massive hemorrhage and acute respiratory distress syndrome. \[5, 8\]  These findings are highly dynamic and can resolve quickly in surviving patients, reflecting the lack of permanent parenchymal damage in many cases. \[22\]

### Ultrasound

Point-of-care lung ultrasound has emerged as a rapid and highly sensitive bedside tool for the diagnosis and monitoring of leptospirosis-associated lung injury. The presence of confluent B-lines, pleural line thickening, and small subpleural consolidations can identify pulmonary hemorrhage before it becomes visible on a standard chest radiograph. This real-time assessment allows for the early initiation of supportive measures, such as protective mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), which is crucial for improving survival in severe cases. \[8, 22\]  Abdominal ultrasound is also useful at the bedside to assess for hepatosplenomegaly or to exclude other causes of acute abdominal pain and jaundice, such as acalculous cholecystitis or pancreatitis, which are increasingly recognized as atypical manifestations of the disease. \[5\]

### MRI

In cases where neurological symptoms are present, MRI of the brain or spine may be indicated. While often unremarkable in aseptic meningitis, MRI can detect rare but severe complications such as polyradiculitis, adhesive arachnoiditis, or intracranial microhemorrhages. \[23\]  These findings are typically associated with the immune phase of the illness and can help guide the use of adjunctive therapies like systemic corticosteroids. \[22, 23\]

## Histologic Findings

Histological examination is not routinely performed during the clinical management of acute leptospirosis but remains a definitive tool for post-mortem diagnosis and for understanding the underlying pathology of multi-organ failure. In the lungs, the most striking finding is widespread alveolar hemorrhage and interstitial edema. Microscopic analysis typically reveals focal or diffuse intra-alveolar erythrocytes, often accompanied by fibrin deposition and the formation of hyaline membranes, consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome. Grossly, the lungs exhibit diffuse subpleural petechiae and ecchymoses, often referred to as a "snowflake" appearance when visualized on imaging, which reflects the underlying microscopic capillary disruption. \[5, 8\]

Renal histology in severe cases is characterized by acute interstitial nephritis and acute tubular necrosis. The interstitium typically demonstrates an inflammatory infiltrate consisting primarily of lymphocytes, monocytes, and plasma cells, while the tubular cells may show swelling, vacuolization, and detachment from the basement membrane. Pathogenic _Leptospira_ can sometimes be visualized within the tubular lumen or interstitium using silver stains, such as the Warthin-Starry or Steiner stains, although immunohistochemistry is significantly more sensitive and specific for identifying leptospiral antigens in fixed tissues. \[1, 7\]

Liver pathology is often less dramatic than the clinical degree of jaundice would suggest. The most consistent findings include centrilobular congestion, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, and the disruption of the intercellular junctions between hepatocytes. Unlike viral hepatitis, massive hepatocellular necrosis is typically absent. Instead, the primary lesion appears to be the loss of the "tight junctions" that normally sequester bile, leading to its leakage into the sinusoidal space. In severe cardiac involvement, histologic examination may reveal interstitial myocarditis with focal areas of necrosis and a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate, explaining the clinical occurrence of arrhythmias and sudden hemodynamic collapse in fulminant cases. \[1, 5\]

## Other Tests

Electrocardiography is a vital bedside test for all patients with severe leptospirosis, as cardiac involvement is common and often underrecognized. Abnormalities are seen in the majority of hospitalized patients and include sinus tachycardia, non-specific ST-T wave changes, and varying degrees of atrioventricular (AV) block. \[5, 24\]  Atrial arrhythmias, particularly new-onset atrial fibrillation, are significant markers of severity and are associated with increased mortality, especially in patients requiring advanced respiratory support such as ECMO. \[25\]

Additionally, a slit-lamp examination is indicated for patients who develop ocular symptoms, as immune-mediated uveitis can present weeks or even months after the resolution of the acute illness. \[1, 5\]

## Procedures

Diagnostic procedures are primarily indicated for patients presenting with severe or localized manifestations of leptospirosis. Lumbar puncture should be performed in any patient with signs of meningismus to evaluate for aseptic meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) typically demonstrates a lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and slightly elevated protein levels. \[5, 7\]  During the first week of illness, _Leptospira_ DNA can often be detected in CSF via PCR.

In cases of suspected leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage may be used to confirm the presence of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, which is characterized by increasingly bloody returns from sequential lavage aliquots. \[8, 22\]

While kidney or liver biopsies are not standard for acute management, they may be considered in cases of diagnostic uncertainty to identify characteristic interstitial nephritis or the disruption of hepatocellular junctions. \[1, 7\]
